extracted.intended_audience: Creators submitting to Summer of Math Exposition (SoME) and peer-review judges (especially teachers/TAs/tutors)
extracted.subtask_description: Rules and evaluation guidance for awarding five $1,000 SoME prizes to entries judged especially helpful for classroom teaching; describes how submitters tag course relevance and how teachers provide a separate classroom-usefulness score that the organizer will use when choosing winners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Helpfulness to struggling students (primary selection question)
rubrics_metrics.description: The central question guiding prize allocation: 'How likely is it that there will be a struggling student whose life becomes easier because they found this piece?'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the organizer's main criterion when deciding which entries receive prize money. The organizer will consider how well a piece would help struggling students, irrespective of course level; teacher scores for classroom usefulness will feed into this judgment along with the organizer's own viewing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classroom relevance / course alignment (submitter tagging)
rubrics_metrics.description: Submitters may add tags to their entry to mark which courses the content might be relevant to.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tags make it easy for teacher-judges to identify pieces aligned to courses they've taught; an entry should be tagged when the creator believes it may be relevant to a particular class.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teacher-assessed classroom-helpfulness (separate scoring category)
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer-review judges who mark themselves as teachers can, for each piece, give a separate score indicating how helpful that piece would be for their classroom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This teacher-specific score is entirely separate from the usual peer review score and is not used in the peer review rankings; the organizer will use these teacher scores (together with their own judgment) when awarding the special classroom-focused prizes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teacher eligibility / self-identification
rubrics_metrics.description: People marking themselves as 'teacher' may specify what kind (e.g., teaching assistant, tutor) and whether they are currently teaching or taught in the past.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When enrolling as a peer-review judge, teachers provide details before casting their first vote (what courses they have taught). This information contextualizes their classroom-helpfulness scores.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peer-review general quality (community ranking)
rubrics_metrics.description: General peer review scores and reviews determine the contest's peer-review rankings and surface broadly thought-provoking/enriching pieces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although the peer review system continues to rank and surface top entries (and the organizer will still highlight highly ranked pieces), the classroom-helpfulness teacher scores are recorded separately for the prize decision; prize money aims to reward valuable contributions that might not bubble to the top of peer rankings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of visual explanations and showing why concepts work
rubrics_metrics.description: Content should provide visual explanations that show why concepts work, not just how to perform procedures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teachers emphasized the need for visual intuition; effective pieces make abstract ideas concrete and show the reasoning behind rules rather than only demonstrating manipulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity and accessible language ('normal words' / avoid jargon)
rubrics_metrics.description: Expositions should use 'normal words' rather than mathematical jargon to be accessible to students.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teachers requested that content be pitched in clear language appropriate for the intended student audience; avoiding unnecessary technical terms helps make lessons classroom-friendly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Connecting concepts to real-world applications and motivation
rubrics_metrics.description: Content should connect mathematical operations to real-world applications and provide motivation for why a topic matters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teachers want students to see why topics matter and to relate abstract concepts to contexts students care about; motivating examples improve classroom usefulness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explicit treatment of common mistakes and student misconceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Good classroom-oriented content shows mistakes and common student errors to address misconceptions directly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Including common pitfalls, typical incorrect reasoning, and corrections helps teachers use the material to preempt or remediate student misunderstandings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical classroom usability (works well as a lesson)
rubrics_metrics.description: Material should be suitable for classroom settings — usable by teachers in lessons rather than only appealing to math enthusiasts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This includes considerations like pacing, examples that transfer to classroom activities, and formats that teachers can incorporate into instruction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate topical and level alignment (foundation → advanced)
rubrics_metrics.description: Entries should align clearly with a target level or course (e.g., foundation-level ages 11–16 topics, intermediate topics like trigonometry/calculus, or advanced topics like linear algebra applications).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The system's tagging plus teacher self-reporting allows teacher-judges to evaluate based on course relevance; the organizer is agnostic to specific course/level but will use alignment information when assessing classroom impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pedagogical aim: make abstract concepts feel inventable / intuitive
rubrics_metrics.description: Strong classroom expositions aim to make abstract concepts concrete and to let students feel that they 'could have invented' the ideas rather than merely memorizing rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teachers highlighted that fostering intuitive understanding and ownership is a key desideratum; pieces that enable students to reconstruct ideas intuitively are valued.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus topics teachers requested (priority areas)
rubrics_metrics.description: Teachers identified high-priority topics that would benefit from better exposition (e.g., variables/algebra, fractions, negative multiplication, ratio/proportion, trigonometry intuition, complex numbers, logarithms, statistics/probability, linear algebra applications, calculus concepts, differential equations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While not strict requirements, submissions that address these commonly-requested areas and do so with classroom-friendly pedagogy may be especially likely to receive teacher support in scoring.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prize allocation mechanics (quantity and amount)
rubrics_metrics.description: The organizer will award $1,000 to five separate entries based on teacher scores and the organizer's judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teacher classroom-helpfulness scores will be considered but are not the sole determinant; the organizer will review data and watch entries before deciding. The teacher score is a separate metric from peer-review rankings.
